title: Indicators of Malicious Activity

header.html: 2.5 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity
the official CompTIA Security+ SY0-801 V8 exam objectives, document version 2.0

toc.title: Network, physical and social engineering attacks

html:
1Malware attacks

Type What it does Key clue
Ransomware Encrypts files and demands payment Files renamed or locked, ransom note
Trojan Looks useful but hides malicious code Does not self-spread
Worm Spreads on its own across the network Rapid spread, no user action
Virus Attaches to a file and spreads when it is run Needs a host file and user action
Spyware Secretly gathers information Hidden data collection
Adware Shows unwanted ads Pop-ups, browser changes
Rootkit Hides itself and other malware at a deep level Tools report nothing wrong
Keylogger Records keystrokes Stolen passwords
Logic bomb Code that runs on a trigger (date, event) Fires when a condition is met
Fileless malware Runs in memory using legitimate tools No file on disk
Exam tip

. Worm spreads by itself; virus needs a host and a user; Trojan pretends to be legitimate. Logic bomb waits for a condition. Rootkit = hides.

2Network, physical and social engineering attacks

Group Attacks
Network attacks DDoS (many sources flood a target), protocol downgrade, rogue access points or devices, sniffing, spoofing, on-path (formerly man-in-the-middle), DNS attacks and cache poisoning
Physical attacks Tailgating (following in), shoulder surfing, skimming (card readers), forced entry
Social engineering Phishing (email), smishing (SMS), vishing (voice), spear phishing (targeted), whaling (executives), quishing (QR codes), impersonation, deepfake (AI-generated voice, video or images)

Exam tip

. Match the channel: smishing = SMS, vishing = voice, quishing = QR, whaling = executives, spear phishing = one person or group. A deepfake is a fake voice or video made by AI.

3Indicators of compromise (IoCs)

Indicator What to look for
Hash A file hash that matches known malware
IP address Traffic to known bad addresses
Domain Lookups of malicious domains
Malicious processes Unknown or misnamed processes
File system artifacts New files, changed system files
Timestamp Activity at odd hours or altered timestamps
Log manipulation Deleted or edited logs
Excessive resource consumption High CPU, memory, disk or network use
Plaintext strings Readable commands or secrets in memory
Account lockout Many failed attempts locking accounts
Impossible travel Sign-ins from far apart places in a short time
Concurrent sessions Same account active in several places

4Application and credential attacks

Attack Meaning
Injection Untrusted input changes a command (SQL injection)
Buffer overflow Input overruns memory, can run attacker code
Replay A captured valid request is sent again
Privilege escalation A user gains higher rights
Forgery Fake requests, such as cross-site request forgery or server-side request forgery
Directory traversal ../ in a path reaches files outside the web folder
Password spraying One or few common passwords tried against many accounts
Brute force Many guesses against one account
User enumeration Finding valid usernames from different error messages
MFA bypass Defeating the second factor, for example push fatigue
Exam tip

. Spraying = few passwords, many accounts (avoids lockout). Brute force = many passwords, one account. Impossible travel and concurrent sessions point to stolen credentials.

5Exam Q&A

5.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1Fabrikam Outdoors sees one worker's laptop files renamed with a new extension and a note demanding payment. Which malware is this?

  • AAdware
  • BKeylogger
  • CLogic bomb
  • DRansomware
Show the answer

Answer: D. Encrypting files and demanding payment is ransomware.

S2Many accounts show a single failed sign-in each, all using the password "Summer2026!". Which attack is this?

  • ABrute force
  • BPassword spraying
  • CReplay
  • DDirectory traversal
Show the answer

Answer: B. Trying one common password across many accounts is password spraying.

S3An employee gets a text claiming to be from the bank with a link to confirm a payment. Which attack is this?

  • AVishing
  • BWhaling
  • CSmishing
  • DSkimming
Show the answer

Answer: C. A malicious text message is smishing.

S4A user's account signs in from Lisbon and ten minutes later from Singapore. Which indicator is this?

  • AAccount lockout
  • BLog manipulation
  • CPlaintext strings
  • DImpossible travel
Show the answer

Answer: D. Two sign-ins from places too far apart for the time are impossible travel.

S5A web request contains ../../etc/passwd in the file name. Which attack is attempted?

  • ADirectory traversal
  • BBuffer overflow
  • CPrivilege escalation
  • DCross-site request forgery
Show the answer

Answer: A. Dot-dot-slash sequences try to reach files outside the intended folder.

S6Malware spreads across the network by itself without any user opening a file. Which type is it?

  • ATrojan
  • BVirus
  • CSpyware
  • DWorm
Show the answer

Answer: D. A worm self-replicates and spreads without user action.

5.2 Recall questions

R1What is the difference between a virus and a worm?

Show the answer

A virus needs a host file and user action; a worm spreads by itself.

R2What is whaling?

Show the answer

Phishing aimed at senior executives.

R3What is a logic bomb?

Show the answer

Malicious code that runs when a condition or date is met.

R4Name three indicators of compromise.

Show the answer

For example impossible travel, log manipulation and excessive resource consumption.

R5What is quishing?

Show the answer

Phishing using QR codes.

R6What is privilege escalation?

Show the answer

Gaining higher rights than intended.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Malware ransomware, Trojan, worm (self-spreads), virus (host), spyware, adware, rootkit (hides), keylogger, logic bomb (trigger), fileless
Network and physical DDoS, downgrade, rogue, sniffing, spoofing, on-path, DNS and cache poisoning; tailgating, shoulder surfing, skimming, forced entry
Social engineering phishing, smishing (SMS), vishing (voice), spear phishing, whaling, quishing (QR), impersonation, deepfake
IoCs hash, IP, domain, processes, artifacts, timestamps, log manipulation, resource spikes, lockouts, impossible travel, concurrent sessions
Application and credential injection, overflow, replay, escalation, forgery, traversal; spraying, brute force, enumeration, MFA bypass
